analysis.one_liner: Gives consumers the right to freeze their credit reports, while letting credit bureaus charge fees each time.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it sat in the House Financial Services Committee until the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: After a year in which millions of Americans' credit files were exposed, this bill would have given every consumer a federal right to place a security freeze on their credit report, so lenders could not open new accounts in their name without their say-so. It would also have subjected the big nationwide credit bureaus to federal cybersecurity exams and barred them from putting Social Security numbers in credit reports. But unlike later proposals, it would have let the bureaus charge consumers up to $5 for every freeze, lift, or unfreeze.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers, especially identity theft victims, seniors, minors, and active-duty service members, who would gain a federal right to lock their credit files against fraudulent new accounts. Anyone whose personal data was exposed in a breach could freeze all three bureaus' reports with defined timelines for placement and removal.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a federal right for any consumer to place a security freeze on their nationwide credit report, with the bureau required to act within 5 business days and lift or remove a freeze within 3 business days on request.
Waives all freeze fees for identity theft victims with a police report, for consumers 65 or older and minors on initial placement and removal, and for active-duty service members with their orders.
Subjects the large nationwide credit bureaus to federal cybersecurity supervision and examination by a designated banking agency.

Bars the big credit bureaus from putting a consumer's Social Security number in any credit report or using it to identify the consumer, effective January 1, 2020, and requires written confirmation of any change to a consumer's name, birth date, Social Security number, or address while a freeze is in place.
Requires the bureaus to notify consumers in writing before removing a freeze the consumer did not request, and lets parents or guardians freeze the files of children under 16 and protected adults.

analysis.who_pays: Credit bureaus would lose the ability to sell consumers' files for new credit without permission and would face new federal cybersecurity exams, though they could recoup some of that by charging consumers up to $5 per freeze, lift, or removal at each bureau. Lenders would face extra friction on new credit applications from frozen applicants.

drawbacks.text: The bill lets credit bureaus charge consumers up to $5 for each freeze, temporary lift, or removal; because a full freeze and unfreeze requires acting at each of the three nationwide bureaus, a consumer could pay up to $45 per cycle for the very protection the bill grants.

A freeze blocks new credit automatically, so consumers who forget to lift it before applying for a mortgage, car loan, apartment, job, or cellphone would face delays; third parties may treat those applications as incomplete.

The ban on using Social Security numbers in credit reports, effective January 1, 2020, would force the bureaus and lenders to rework how they match consumers to files, a significant operational cost that could cause matching errors during the transition.

The freeze comes with broad exceptions: existing creditors, their affiliates and debt collectors, insurers, employers, landlords and background screeners, and government agencies can still access the file, so a freeze stops new-account fraud but not every use of the data.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: a federal right to lock your credit file is one of the strongest tools against new-account identity theft, and the free freeze for victims, seniors, minors, and service members targets the people most at risk. But the fee structure is a serious flaw. Charging consumers up to $5 per action at each of three bureaus turns a protection into a pay-to-play right, and the bill's timelines and wide list of exceptions mean the freeze is not airtight. A version of this idea enacted later in the same Congress dropped the fees; this draft kept them.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in October 2017 and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which never scheduled a hearing or markup, so it died when the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Patrick McHenry introduced the bill on October 12, 2017, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services.
No further action of any kind, including no hearing, markup, or floor vote, appears in the bill's action history for the remainder of the 115th Congress.
The bill drew one cosponsor, a Republican, and never advanced past the committee referral stage.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The credit bureaus, which avoided the cybersecurity exams, the Social Security number ban, and even the fee-capped freeze regime this bill would have imposed; consumers gained nothing from this version, though freeze protections resurfaced in later legislation.

for.name: Rep. Patrick T. McHenry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it was referred to his committee.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: The only legislative record is a Republican sponsor with one Republican cosponsor and no votes, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.industry: Nationwide credit reporting agencies (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion)
industries.note: The bill would both restrict and entrench them: a consumer freeze right and a ban on Social Security numbers in reports cut into their core business of selling files for new credit, and they would face federal cybersecurity exams. At the same time, the bill makes them the permanent gatekeepers of the freeze system and hands them explicit authority to charge consumers up to $5 per freeze, lift, or removal.

Lenders would face friction: applications from frozen consumers could be treated as incomplete and delayed until the freeze is lifted, and the Social Security number ban would force changes to how they verify applicants. They would also benefit from fewer fraudulent new accounts.

A federal freeze right gives consumers a free-of-charge alternative tool, though the bill preserves access for paid monitoring subscriptions and keeps monitoring upsells alive through the freeze confirmation process.
